title: A map, not a wall
hook: four pillars: what we believe, how we celebrate, how we live, how we pray

segments.voice: Yesterday, what Merton gives: holiness as becoming who you are before God. Your line was become who you are. What did you do on purpose? Today, a new part of the path, and a big book. Day two hundred ninety.

Picture the thickest book on a Catholic family's shelf. Not the Bible, the other one. Heavy, a little intimidating, full of numbered paragraphs, the kind of thing people assume is a list of rules. Maybe you've seen one in a parish office, or on a relative's nightstand with a rosary on top. A lot of people have never opened it, because they think it's a wall: a list of everything you can't do. It's actually built more like a map. Today: the catechism.
screen: `THE OTHER BIG BOOK ON THE SHELF.` → `A LIST OF RULES?` → `BUILT MORE LIKE A MAP.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Catechism comes from a Greek verb, katechein, built on the word for sound, as in echo. It means to teach by word of mouth, to make something resound in someone's ear. Luke uses it at the start of his Gospel, telling a man named Theophilus he writes so that, in the Douay-Rheims, "thou mayest know the verity of those words in which thou hast been instructed." Instructed there is that echo word. The faith was passed on out loud long before it was printed. Second, the book. There have been many catechisms. After the Council of Trent came the Roman Catechism in 1566. American Catholics grew up for generations on the Baltimore Catechism, with its famous opening questions: Who made us? God made us. Why did God make us? To know him, to love him, to serve him, and to be happy with him forever. In 1992, Pope John Paul II released the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the one on shelves today: two thousand eight hundred sixty-five numbered paragraphs. Third, the four pillars. It's built in four parts. What Catholics believe: the Creed. How they celebrate: the liturgy and the seven sacraments. How they live: life in Christ, the commandments and the virtues. And how they pray: ending with the Our Father. Belief, worship, life, prayer. Fourth, why a map. The Catechism isn't meant to be read cover to cover like a rulebook. It's meant to show how everything connects: why a belief shapes a sacrament, why a sacrament shapes a life, why a life turns into prayer. For the next weeks, we'll walk it, one theme at a time.
screen: `KATECHEIN — TO MAKE IT ECHO.` · `TRENT, BALTIMORE, THEN 1992.` · `BELIEVE, CELEBRATE, LIVE, PRAY.` · `EVERYTHING CONNECTS.` · then, large: `FOUR PILLARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand among the four pillars. Settle and breathe. Picture four stone columns holding up a roof. Touch the first: what you believe, or wonder about. The second: how you celebrate, a Mass, a feast, a candle. The third: how you live, one choice today. The fourth: how you pray, or how you'd like to. Notice which pillar feels strongest in your life right now, and which feels thin. No judgment. Just notice. If you pray, you can ask for help with the thin one. The bell holds the time.
Catechism. From the Greek for making something echo: a summary of the faith, taught aloud and passed on. Today's Catechism has four pillars. Today's word.
Your line: four pillars. Today, if you can, look up the Catechism's table of contents online and just read the four part titles. Believe, celebrate, live, pray. Day two hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Catholics use the Catechism of the Catholic Church as a reference for teaching the faith, and parishes build their classes for children, teens and adults joining the Church around its four parts.
